routes.description: Establish Christian theism as the best cumulative explanation of cosmological, fine-tuning, moral, historical, and experiential evidence.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the principal evidence families materially favor a personal, morally good creator revealed through Jesus over skeptical atheism.

motionBridge.description: The cumulative evidence makes Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism.

centralBridges.description: The universe began and therefore has a transcendent personal cause.
Life-permitting fine-tuning is better explained by intelligent design than necessity or chance.
Objective moral values and duties exist and require God as their ontological ground.
The principal historical facts concerning Jesus are best explained by his resurrection.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Sincere immediate experience can provide properly basic awareness of God.
A timeless immaterial cause is more plausibly an unembodied mind than an abstract object.

routes.description: Show that Craig's evidence is too uncertain, underdetermining, or naturally explicable to justify the specific Christian God hypothesis.
routes.successCriteria: Defeat enough indispensable evidential bridges that skeptical atheism remains more reasonable than accepting the specific Christian God hypothesis.

motionBridge.description: The presented evidence does not justify preferring Christian theism to skeptical atheism.

centralBridges.description: Cosmological evidence and causal intuitions underdetermine a beginning, transcendent cause, or mind.
Fine-tuning probabilities and designer inferences are premature and do not identify the Christian God.
Moral realism and intrinsic value are available without positing a divine ontological ground.
Dependent late religious sources and ordinary psychology weaken the resurrection inference.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Conflicting culturally transmitted religions undermine religious experience as a reliable method.
Sincere nonbelief and unclear evidence count against the proposed loving, relationship-seeking God.

sections.title: Cosmic beginning, causation, and a personal cause
sections.rationale: This sustained exchange tests the beginning premise, causal principle, and inference from a nonphysical cause to an unembodied mind.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: A finite cosmic past and the Borde-Guth-Vilenkin result support an absolute beginning, which requires a transcendent immaterial personal cause.

sourceSpan.excerpt: past events must be finite in number; therefore the universe began to exist and has a transcendent cause

proMoves.attributionBasis: The span occurs continuously within Craig's identified opening presentation and follows his announced first argument.

response.rationale: This is Craig's initial affirmative cosmological case and therefore has no earlier selected argumentative target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The syllogistic route is explicit, but the transitions among local universe, global universe, spacetime boundary, and absolute beginning remain partly compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Craig acknowledges speculative models and missing quantum gravity, but presents the absolute-beginning and personal-cause conclusions more strongly than those caveats warrant.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The core syllogism is valid, but the beginning-to-personal-cause route contains material modal and candidate-exhaustiveness bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The theorem and philosophical examples provide relevant support, though their reach to an absolute beginning and personal agency is incompletely defended.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive, it clearly advances the announced cosmological route without needing to answer a prior selected move.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the declared central cosmology bridge and is rated within the central tier band.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops Craig's own case without substantively reconstructing a live opposing alternative.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 155–251 contain the finite-past argument, BGV appeal, causal syllogism, divine-attribute derivation, and mind-versus-abstract-object inference.

conMoves.speaker: Peter Millican
conMoves.proposition: Experience does not license creation-ex-nihilo causation, current cosmology does not establish an absolute global beginning, and a nonphysical cause need not be a mind.

sourceSpan.excerpt: I cannot infer from my own experience that creation from nothing is causal in the same way; the theorem proves less than Bill needs

conMoves.attributionBasis: The span is within Millican's identified opening case and explicitly introduces and criticizes Craig's Kalam premises.

components.text: The global universe had an absolute temporal beginning.
Whatever begins ex nihilo must have a transcendent cause.
The nonphysical cause must be an unembodied mind.

response.rationale: Millican separately challenges the absolute-beginning evidence, the extrapolation of causation to creation ex nihilo, and the restricted inference to an unembodied mind.

precisionFindings.rationale: Millican explicitly distinguishes local from global universe and separates the causal, temporal, and mental-substance objections.

calibrationFindings.rationale: He frames the conclusion as doubt and underdetermination, repeatedly emphasizing the limitations of current physics and human experience.

charity.alternative: Craig's strongest case combines a philosophical finite-past argument, BGV cosmology, a causal principle, and elimination of nonmental candidates.
charity.decisiveQualification: BGV concerns average expansion and does not by itself exclude every prior contracting or unknown physical regime.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reply consistently separates the premises and shows why each inferential extension requires additional support.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It uses relevant cosmological qualifications and experiential limits, though the quantum-particle characterization and some scientific claims remain compressed.

responsiveness.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts all three indispensable components of the selected cosmological case, including its decisive beginning premise.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the pro route's central cosmology bridge and is rated within the central tier band.

representationalCharity.rationale: Millican reconstructs the valid Kalam form and distinguishes its stages before disputing its premises, with only minor compression of Craig's modal defense.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 775–973 present the Kalam form, objections from causal experience, composition, local/global cosmology, BGV limitations, and the unsupported-mind objection.

sections.title: Fine-tuning and designer inference
sections.rationale: The exchange directly contests whether life-permitting parameters support design and whether any designer inference favors the Christian God.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: Life-permitting constants and initial conditions display extreme improbability plus an independent pattern, favoring design over necessity or chance.

sourceSpan.excerpt: there are only three possible explanations of this extraordinary fine-tuning: physical necessity, chance, or design

proMoves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly labels fine-tuning as his second opening argument and delivers this uninterrupted inference.

response.rationale: This is the first selected statement of Craig's design argument and has no earlier selected target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The explanatory trilemma is recoverable, but the probability space and scope of physical necessity are not fully specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The confident elimination of chance and necessity exceeds the supplied specification of possible values, priors, and rival cosmological explanations.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The design inference is intelligible, but the exhaustive trilemma and independent-pattern bridge remain materially underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Craig identifies constants and initial conditions but provides no detailed probability measure or representative quantitative support in the selected span.

responsiveness.rationale: The opening clearly advances the fine-tuning route without an earlier selected opponent target.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the declared central fine-tuning bridge and stays within the central tier band.

representationalCharity.rationale: No live opposing account is represented in enough detail to test charity.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 286–321 state the necessity-chance-design trilemma, patterned-improbability warrant, and designer conclusion.

conMoves.speaker: Peter Millican
conMoves.proposition: Fine-tuning is intriguing but present physics and probability assignments are too immature, while the data neither establish moral perfection nor fit uniquely with an omnipotent Christian creator.

sourceSpan.excerpt: a physically inexplicable coincidence would invite a cosmic designer, but I also see good reason for caution and modesty

conMoves.attributionBasis: Millican is explicitly reintroduced for this rebuttal and announces that he is addressing the fine-tuning argument.

components.text: The life-permitting range is meaningfully improbable under chance.
Physical necessity and multiverse-style explanations can be excluded.
A designer inference materially favors the Christian God.

response.rationale: Millican grants the conditional force of a genuinely inexplicable coincidence, then challenges the probability base, rival explanations, and bridge from designer to the specific Christian hypothesis.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional concession and distinct objections to probability, physics, moral character, omnipotence, and cosmic scale are clearly delimited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Millican expressly concedes what stronger future evidence could establish and limits his conclusion to present evidential insufficiency.

charity.alternative: If fundamental constants were demonstrably contingent, precisely constrained, and physically inexplicable, they would naturally invite a cosmic-intelligence explanation.
charity.decisiveQualification: That conditional inference would establish at most a powerful designer unless further evidence identified moral perfection and specifically Christian attributes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reply combines a clear conditional concession with independent underdetermination and specificity objections.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It supplies several concrete scientific uncertainties and comparative hypotheses, though some numerical illustrations are not independently defended.

responsiveness.rationale: All indispensable parts of Craig's inference are contacted, including the probability claim, rival explanations, and religious specificity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move attacks the pro route's central fine-tuning bridge and is rated within the central band.

representationalCharity.rationale: Millican states a strong circumstance under which fine-tuning would support cosmic intelligence before explaining the narrower reach of that conclusion.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 1359–1545 include the conditional concession, sample-size and future-physics cautions, multiverse alternative, anti-God comparison, and omnipotence-efficiency objection.

sections.title: Objective morality and divine grounding
sections.rationale: The speakers contest both the existence and interpretation of objective moral facts and whether their ontological ground must be divine.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: Objective moral values and duties exist, while atheistic evolution and conditioning cannot make them objectively binding; therefore God exists as their ground.

sourceSpan.excerpt: if God did not exist objective moral values and duties would not exist; objective moral values and duties do exist

proMoves.attributionBasis: Craig announces this as his third argument during his uninterrupted opening statement.

response.rationale: This is the initial selected formulation of Craig's moral argument and therefore has no earlier target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The syllogism and belief-independent definition are clear, but objective value, duty, bindingness, and ontological grounding are not fully distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The deductive conclusion depends on a controversial grounding premise supported mainly by evolutionary genealogy and selected testimony rather than elimination of secular realism.

charity.alternative: Atheistic naturalism can explain moral belief and cooperative conduct through evolution and social conditioning.
charity.decisiveQualification: Explaining the origin of moral belief does not by itself settle whether secular objective moral truths or reasons exist.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The stated modus-tollens structure is valid, but the move shifts too quickly from naturalistic genealogy to the impossibility of secular normativity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Moral experience and cited opinions are relevant, yet the crucial divine-grounding premise lacks sustained comparison with secular realist accounts.

responsiveness.rationale: The constructive directly advances Craig's moral route and requires no earlier selected response.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It supports the pro route's central morality bridge and is scored within the central tier band.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move treats naturalistic evolutionary accounts as if they exhaust atheistic metaethics, omitting the decisive secular-realist qualification.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 322–400 define objective morality, give an evolutionary genealogy, appeal to moral apprehension, and infer God from the two premises.

conMoves.speaker: Peter Millican
conMoves.proposition: Many nontheists are moral realists, and neither moral perception nor human intrinsic value becomes intelligible only by adding an undetected divine ground.

sourceSpan.excerpt: 56.3 percent were moral realists but only 14.6 percent were theists, so there are plenty of moral realists who are not theists

conMoves.attributionBasis: The chair has returned the floor to Millican, who explicitly identifies moral realism as the issue under discussion.

components.text: Objective moral values and duties cannot exist without God.
Moral experience reliably establishes objective values and duties.

response.rationale: Millican directly contests the indispensable divine-grounding premise but does not defeat Craig's separate appeal to moral experience; indeed, he largely accepts moral realism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The grounding objection is clear, though Millican openly notes that the word objective bundles several meanings he has not fully resolved.

calibrationFindings.rationale: He presents the survey as pressure against Craig's premise rather than proof and admits difficulty giving a universally persuasive account of value.

charity.alternative: Craig distinguishes atheists' ability to know moral truths from the ontological question of what makes those truths objectively binding.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing that nontheists believe moral realism does not by itself supply the ontology Craig demands.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conceptual challenge is coherent, although the appeal to philosophers' views is not itself an ontological explanation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The survey and examples establish live secular realism but only partially warrant the stronger claim that divine grounding is unnecessary.

responsiveness.rationale: The reply contacts the decisive grounding premise but leaves Craig's independent moral-experience premise substantially intact.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the pro route's central morality bridge and is rated in the central tier band.

representationalCharity.rationale: Millican explicitly recognizes Craig's epistemology-versus-ontology distinction before challenging the latter.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 1928–2010 cite the philosopher survey, distinguish moral knowledge from ontology, question objective's meaning, and develop the atheist-perception analogy.

sections.title: Resurrection evidence and natural explanation
sections.rationale: This issue tests the specifically Christian bridge: whether the historical sources establish facts whose best explanation is a divine resurrection.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: The empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and disciples' unexpected resurrection belief are widely accepted facts best explained by Jesus rising from the dead.

sourceSpan.excerpt: there are actually three facts recognized by the majority of historians today which I believe are best explained by the resurrection

proMoves.attributionBasis: Craig labels this his fourth opening argument and enumerates the three historical claims in a continuous span.

response.rationale: This is Craig's first selected historical argument and therefore has no earlier selected target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The three facts and conclusion are clear, but the scope of scholarly consensus and the comparative class of natural explanations remain underspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that no plausible naturalistic explanation exists is much stronger than the brief consensus citations and dismissal of two alternatives establish.

charity.alternative: Natural explanations include body removal, survival, legendary development, visionary experience, and psychological reinforcement.
charity.decisiveQualification: Rejecting selected older alternatives does not exhaust combinations of source dependence, memory, legend, and religious psychology.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference to resurrection is intelligible, but the best-explanation step requires a more complete rival comparison.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Craig names scholars and three data points, yet source independence, dating, consensus scope, and alternative likelihoods receive limited support.

responsiveness.rationale: The constructive directly advances the historical route without a prior selected opponent target.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It supports the pro route's central resurrection bridge and is rated within the central tier band.

representationalCharity.rationale: Naturalistic alternatives are reduced mainly to theft and apparent death, omitting stronger mixed historical and psychological accounts.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 426–470 enumerate the empty tomb, appearances, and transformed belief, cite scholarly opinions, reject two alternatives, and infer resurrection.

conMoves.speaker: Peter Millican
conMoves.proposition: The Gospel accounts are late, interested, mutually dependent, discrepant, and poorly corroborated, so they provide weak grounds for overturning ordinary natural explanations.

sourceSpan.excerpt: four accounts all written many years after the alleged events, not by eyewitnesses but by devoted Christians

conMoves.attributionBasis: Millican explicitly announces that he is turning to the resurrection and delivers the source criticism continuously.

components.text: The three asserted facts have sufficiently strong independent historical attestation.
A literal resurrection explains the evidence better than natural historical development.

response.rationale: Millican attacks the evidential foundation through dating, authorship, dependence, discrepancies, selection, and absent corroboration, thereby challenging both the facts and miracle inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The source-critical proposition and its intended evidential consequence are explicit and consistently bounded to the available Gospel accounts.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The criticisms warrant substantial caution, though several historical claims are asserted rapidly and do not fully analyze Craig's non-Gospel traditions.

charity.alternative: Craig's minimal-facts case relies on claims of broad scholarly acceptance rather than treating every Gospel detail as equally reliable.
charity.decisiveQualification: Discrepancies in secondary details do not automatically defeat the empty tomb, experiences, or subsequent belief.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The connection from dependent, interested, discrepant sources to reduced evidential force is coherent, with a bounded gap concerning minimal facts.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete dependence and corroboration issues support skepticism, though the treatment of dating and all relevant traditions is compressed.

responsiveness.rationale: The reply contacts both the factual foundation and best-explanation inference of Craig's selected historical case.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It attacks the pro route's central resurrection bridge and is scored within the central tier band.

representationalCharity.rationale: Millican engages the historical evidence directly but partially conflates criticism of full narratives with Craig's narrower minimal-facts formulation.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 2056–2110 discuss late non-eyewitness authorship, Synoptic dependence, discrepancies, canonical selection, and lack of external corroboration.

sections.title: Religious experience, diversity, and hiddenness
sections.rationale: The final contested family concerns whether immediate experience reliably reveals God despite conflicting religions and sincere, reflective nonbelief.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: God can be known immediately apart from argument, and sincere seekers who draw near to God will encounter an evident divine reality.

sourceSpan.excerpt: you can know that God exists wholly apart from arguments simply by immediately experiencing him

proMoves.attributionBasis: Craig labels personal experience as his fifth consideration in the same identified opening speech.

response.rationale: This is the initial selected experiential claim, offered before Millican's diversity and sincere-seeker objections.

precisionFindings.rationale: Immediate experience is identifiable, but sincere seeking, divine self-disclosure, and the scope of the universal-seeming promise are not operationally delimited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The universal assurance to sincere seekers rests on scriptural promise and reported experience without addressing conflicting or absent experiences.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Immediate acquaintance could in principle justify belief, but the inference from sincerity to guaranteed disclosure lacks a defended bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Biblical testimony and experiential description provide some support but do not establish reliability across conflicting religious experiences.

responsiveness.rationale: The constructive clearly advances the experiential subsidiary route without an earlier selected target.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It supports the declared subsidiary experience bridge and is rated within the subsidiary tier band.

representationalCharity.rationale: The opening experiential claim does not represent a live opposing alternative.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 471–505 distinguish immediate experience from argument, cite John Hick and scripture, and promise disclosure to sincere seekers.

conMoves.speaker: Peter Millican
conMoves.proposition: Conflicting culturally acquired religions make religious experience unreliable, while his own prolonged sincere inquiry ending in nonbelief directly challenges promised disclosure.

sourceSpan.excerpt: if some method of acquiring beliefs leads to lots of different and conflicting beliefs, then that method cannot be relied on

conMoves.attributionBasis: The span occurs in Millican's identified opening presentation and expressly anticipates and rejects the genetic-fallacy interpretation.

components.text: Immediate religious experience is a reliable route to the Christian God.
Every sincere seeker will receive evident divine disclosure.

response.rationale: The selected diversity argument directly attacks experiential reliability, while the later materially developed sincere-seeker testimony supplies the counterexample to guaranteed disclosure.

precisionFindings.rationale: Millican carefully states that dubious origins do not prove falsity and limits his conclusion to the unreliability of the shared belief-forming methods.

calibrationFindings.rationale: He argues for reduced reliability and a strong burden rather than claiming that diversity deductively disproves Christianity.

charity.alternative: Craig combines immediate experience with logic and public evidence rather than relying solely on inherited religious belief.
charity.decisiveQualification: Diversity directly undermines experiential method only to the extent that incompatible traditions use materially similar experiences and transmission processes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move avoids the genetic fallacy and draws the narrower reliability conclusion from incompatible outputs of similar methods.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Geographic variation and conflicting exclusive traditions support the reliability concern, supplemented later by a concrete sincere-seeker counterexample.

responsiveness.rationale: The diversity analysis and later sincere-inquiry development contact both indispensable components of Craig's experiential claim.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It attacks the declared subsidiary experience bridge and is rated at the top of the subsidiary tier band.

representationalCharity.rationale: Millican explicitly denies that origins establish falsity and acknowledges Craig's appeal to logic and evidence, while isolating the experiential reliability issue.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 663–707 provide the strongest diversity-and-reliability formulation; events 2938–2964 materially develop it with Millican's sincere theological search and resulting nonbelief.

pro.rationale: No distinct debate-wide consequence remains outside the selected move ratings, response links, importance assignments, and section weights.

eligibility.completionCriterion: Establish the cumulative pro route to Christian theism.
eligibility.distinctConsequence: No unscored consequence distinct from the five represented evidential routes was identified.
eligibility.counterfactual: Removing the adjustment leaves every identified pro success criterion evaluated by the selected ledger.

con.rationale: No distinct debate-wide consequence remains outside the selected attacks, surviving constructives, response structures, and weighted issue families.

eligibility.completionCriterion: Show that the evidence does not justify preferring Christian theism to skeptical atheism.
eligibility.distinctConsequence: No separate unscored burden consequence survives the existing treatment of underdetermination, morality, history, diversity, and hiddenness.
eligibility.counterfactual: Removing the adjustment leaves the con success criterion fully represented by the selected replies and their surviving objections.
